newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten criticises Beijing's protest ban on HK.
newsitem.headline: Patten criticises Beijing's protest ban on HK.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said on Friday he was unsettled by China's statement that ceremonies in the territory marking the 1989 crushing of democracy protests in Beijing would not be tolerated after 1997.
Such remarks undermined confidence in the territory, Patten said, adding that London had taken up the issue at a high level with Beijing and was waiting for a response.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to Chinese control at midnight on June 30 next year.

Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, in an interview published in The Asian Wall Street Journal on Wednesday, said Hong Kong activists would not be allowed to mark the bloody crackdown on democracy protests in Tiananmen Square.

"In the future, Hong Kong should not hold activities which directly interfere in the affairs of the mainland," Qian said when asked whether China would permit commemorations to continue beyond the handover.
"I think Mr Qian's remarks were deeply unsettling," Patten said during a brief meeting with reporters. "The community has been extremely unsettled and concerned about the remarks.
"The British government has taken up its concern at a high level and we look forward to a response, a response which I hope will set people's minds at rest."
Patten, who leaves for London late on Friday for a week, said he would discuss the matter with British Prime Minister John Major and Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control under the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration which pledges considerable autonomy for Hong Kong and the right to maintain capitalist freedoms for 50 years.
"What Mr Qian appeared to be saying seems to be wholly at variance, wholly at odds with specific stipulations set out in the Joint Declaration," Patten said.
But Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang on Thursday argued Qian's remarks had been "wrongly extended" and marked no shift in Chinese policy on post-handover Hong Kong.
